content: The costs of recent studies conducted in Iraq and Yemen, which covered approximately half of these countries and lasted six months, ranged between $120,000 and $300,000. If an inventory study to directly assess underreporting of TB cases has not been conducted in the past decade, planning for such a survey using WHO guidelines is recommended. If an inventory study reveals significant underreporting of diagnosed cases, immediate action is required. Examples of such strategies include public-private and public-public collaboration models, incentive-based and reimbursement schemes, and mandatory case reporting to align provider practices with national and international standards. Data from inventory studies can also be used to update and correct surveillance estimates. If necessary, key actions to address gaps that hinder achieving the standard should be outlined, along with an estimated budget to support activities bridging these gaps. In the United Kingdom, TB case notification became a legal requirement in 1913. Under the Public Health (Control of Disease) Act of 1984, all forms of TB must be reported by the diagnosing or suspecting physician. Public Health England uses inventory methods to assess whether all TB cases are reported to the national program by matching data with other sources, such as laboratory databases, national HIV surveillance, and specific surveys. These comparisons typically show underreporting rates of 5–17%. A detailed audit in 2006 of unmatched laboratory Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates revealed an underreporting rate of approximately 5%. Lessons learned from inventory studies have been applied to improve data quality in the national web-based case reporting system. In the UK, both benchmarks for TB surveillance are satisfied, and the standard is met. In Iraq, TB is a notifiable disease. An inventory study conducted in 2011 assessed the level of TB underreporting. Prospective longitudinal surveillance was implemented for all eligible public and private non-NTP (National Tuberculosis Program) providers in a random sample of eight out of 18 Iraqi governorates over three months. Non-NTP facilities were provided with forms identical to those used by the NTP to record demographic, diagnostic, referral, and treatment information. Data linkage revealed a 16% underreporting rate. Findings indicated the need to strengthen TB surveillance in Iraq to reduce underreporting. While the first benchmark was satisfied, the second was not, meaning the standard was not met. This requires widespread availability of healthcare services with qualified staff capable of recognizing TB symptoms and diagnostic capabilities, such as laboratory testing and radiography. Barriers to accessing these services, including geographic, financial, and quality-related issues, must be minimal. Indicators such as under-five mortality rates, life expectancy, maternal mortality ratios, healthcare workforce density, antenatal care coverage, and out-of-pocket health expenditures are used to assess health system coverage and performance. For TB surveillance, two benchmarks are critical: an under-five mortality rate below 10 per 1,000 live births and out-of-pocket health expenditures below 25% of total health expenditures. Countries meeting these benchmarks are considered to have good access to healthcare. For example, in 2010, the Netherlands met both benchmarks with an under-five mortality rate of 4 per 1,000 live births and out-of-pocket health expenditures at 5% of total health expenditures. Conversely, countries like Brazil, China, India, and Kenya did not meet either benchmark, indicating significant gaps in healthcare access and quality. Thailand partially met the standard, satisfying the second benchmark but falling slightly short of the first. The United Kingdom and the United States met both benchmarks, demonstrating high-quality healthcare systems. Vital registration systems with high national coverage and quality are essential for accurately documenting TB-related mortality. High-quality data on causes of death are critical for monitoring TB burden, informing policy decisions, and allocating resources effectively. However, many countries lack optimal vital registration systems, leading to underreporting of TB mortality. To address this, countries can use sample vital registration systems, mortality surveys, or demographic surveillance systems with verbal autopsy to improve TB mortality estimates. Training healthcare personnel, harmonizing death certification processes, and increasing public awareness of the importance of death registration are recommended actions to enhance data quality. Surveillance of drug-resistant TB is crucial for understanding TB epidemiology, monitoring trends, assessing NTP performance, and designing effective treatment regimens. Surveillance systems based on routine diagnostic testing or representative surveys of previously untreated TB cases are the preferred methods. For example, in Latvia, an electronic TB surveillance system documented rifampicin susceptibility for 80% of new pulmonary TB cases, meeting the standard. In Bangladesh, routine diagnostic testing is used for drug resistance surveillance, but further strengthening of laboratory capacity is needed to meet WHO recommendations. Countries without drug resistance surveillance data should plan nationally representative surveys and transition to routine diagnostic testing systems. This requires investments in laboratory capacity and integration of drug resistance testing into NTP strategies and financial plans.
